meta.title: The models themselves
meta.note: The heuristics page tells you which family a problem belongs to. This page shows you what to actually draw for each one, with the numbers worked all the way through. Every calculation here has been checked.
meta.howToRead: Each model has: the words that tell you it is this one, the bar model drawn, a worked example with every step, and the mistake that this particular model invites.

drawing.title: Five rules for drawing any model

rules.r: One unit is one unit everywhere.
rules.w: If a box means 1 unit at the top of the page, it means 1 unit at the bottom. Boxes drawn different sizes for the same unit is the single commonest reason a model gives the wrong answer.
Comparison only reads correctly if both bars start from the same edge. The bit sticking out on the right is then the difference, and you can see it.

rules.r: Label the bar, not just the box.
rules.w: Write who or what each bar is at the left end. Two unlabelled bars three minutes later are two bars you no longer understand.

rules.r: Mark the question with a question mark.
rules.w: Put a ? on the exact thing being asked for, before you calculate anything. It stops you answering the step instead of the question.

rules.r: Draw the after picture underneath the before picture.
rules.w: Never redraw over the top. You need both to compare, and the comparison is where the answer is.

models.name: Part-whole
models.when: A total is given or asked for, and nothing is being compared.
models.draw: One bar cut into parts. The whole bar is the total. Put the brace above for the total, and label each part.

example.q: A shop has 120 books. 45 are novels and 30 are comics. The rest are textbooks. How many textbooks are there?
steps: Draw one bar for all 120 books, and cut it into three parts.
Novels and comics together: 45 + 30 = 75
Textbooks are what is left: 120 − 75 = 45

models.trap: Being asked for the whole and giving a part, or the other way round. Mark the ? before you start.

models.name: Comparison
models.when: Two quantities are set against each other and a difference is mentioned.
models.draw: Two bars, one above the other, left ends lined up. The bit sticking out on the right is the difference.

example.q: Ali has 27 more stickers than Ben. Ben has 57 stickers. How many do they have altogether?
steps: Draw Ben's bar. Draw Ali's bar directly above it, longer, with the extra bit labelled 27.
Altogether: 84 + 57 = 141

models.trap: Reading the comparison backwards. Ali has 27 more than Ben means Ali's bar is the longer one. Say the sentence aloud while you draw the longer bar.

models.name: Units, or multiples
models.when: One quantity is a whole number of times another.
models.draw: Draw the SMALLER quantity as one unit. The larger is that many equal units, drawn the same size each.

example.q: Ravi has three times as many marbles as Meiling. Together they have 96 marbles. How many does Ravi have?
steps: Meiling is 1 unit. Ravi is 3 units, drawn as three equal boxes.
Total units: 1 + 3 = 4 units
4 units = 96, so 1 unit = 96 ÷ 4 = 24
Ravi is 3 units: 3 × 24 = 72

models.trap: Drawing the big one as one unit. Always make the smaller quantity the unit, or you end up dividing by a fraction.

models.name: Fraction of a whole
models.when: A fraction is applied to a whole quantity.
models.draw: Cut the bar into as many equal parts as the bottom number of the fraction. Shade the top number of them.

example.q: Siti spent two-fifths of her $60 on a book. How much had she left?
steps: Cut the bar into 5 equal units, because the bottom number is 5.
5 units = $60, so 1 unit = $12
She spent 2 units: 2 × $12 = $24
She has 3 units left: 3 × $12 = $36

models.trap: Answering the part that was spent when the question asked what was left.

models.name: Fraction of the remainder
models.when: A second fraction is taken, but of what is LEFT rather than of the original.
models.draw: Cut the bar for the first fraction. Then cut ONLY the leftover section for the second fraction. Never cut the whole bar twice.

example.q: Raju spent one-third of his money on a game, then gave half of the remainder to his sister. He had $45 left. How much did he start with?
steps: Cut the whole bar into 3 units. He spends 1 unit, so 2 units remain.
Now cut only that remainder in half. Half of 2 units is 1 unit, so he gives away 1 unit.
What is left is 1 unit, and that is $45.
He started with 3 units: 3 × $45 = $135

models.trap: Cutting the whole bar in half for the second fraction. Half the remainder is not half the total. This is the most-tested trap in the whole of P6 fractions.

models.name: Units and parts (ratio)
models.when: A relationship is given as a ratio, or as a fraction comparing two people.
models.draw: One box per unit for each person, all boxes the same size. Write the number of units at the end of each bar.

example.q: Amy and Bala share 176 stickers in the ratio 3 : 5. How many more does Bala get?
steps: Amy is 3 units, Bala is 5 units. Total 8 units.
8 units = 176, so 1 unit = 176 ÷ 8 = 22
The difference is 5 − 3 = 2 units

models.trap: Working out both amounts and then subtracting, when the difference in units gets you there in one step. Both work, but the extra steps are where errors creep in.

models.name: Ratio with the total unchanged
models.when: Something moves from one person to the other and nobody else is involved.
models.draw: Two ratios, before and after. Make the TOTAL number of units the same in both by scaling, because the total has not changed.

example.q: The ratio of Pam's stamps to Quek's was 3 : 2. Pam gave Quek 21 stamps and the ratio became 4 : 5. How many did Pam have at first?
steps: Before, the total is 3 + 2 = 5 parts. After, the total is 4 + 5 = 9 parts. The total has not changed, so scale both to 45 parts.
Before becomes 27 : 18. After becomes 20 : 25.
Pam went from 27 units to 20 units, a drop of 7 units, and that drop is the 21 stamps.
7 units = 21, so 1 unit = 3
Pam at first: 27 units = 27 × 3 = 81

models.trap: Treating the units before and after as the same size without scaling. They are not, because the two ratios have different totals. Making the totals match is the whole method.

models.name: Ratio with the difference unchanged
models.when: The same amount is added to both, or taken from both, or time passes for two ages.
models.draw: Two ratios, before and after. Make the DIFFERENCE in units the same in both by scaling, because the gap has not changed.

example.q: The ratio of a son's age to his father's is 2 : 5. In 12 years it will be 3 : 6. How old is the son now?
steps: Ages: the gap between them never changes. Before, the gap is 5 − 2 = 3 parts. After, the gap is 6 − 3 = 3 parts. They already match, so no scaling is needed.
The son goes from 2 units to 3 units, a rise of 1 unit, and that rise is the 12 years.
1 unit = 12
Son now: 2 units = 24

models.trap: Using the total instead of the difference. When the same amount is added to both, the total changes but the gap does not. Ask which one is protected before you scale.

models.name: Ratio with one quantity unchanged
models.when: Only one of the two amounts changes; the other is never touched.
models.draw: Two ratios, before and after. Scale so that the UNCHANGED person has the same number of units in both.

example.q: The ratio of Ann's beads to Ben's was 2 : 3. Ann bought 30 more beads and the ratio became 4 : 3. Ben's number never changed. How many did Ann have at first?
steps: Ben is untouched, so his units must mean the same thing in both lines. He is 3 in both already, so no scaling is needed.
Ann goes from 2 units to 4 units, a rise of 2 units, and that rise is the 30 beads.
2 units = 30, so 1 unit = 15
Ann at first: 2 units = 30

models.trap: Scaling to the total when only one person changed. Here the total is not protected and the difference is not protected; the fixed person is. Always scale to whatever cannot have changed.

models.name: Percentage
models.when: Any percentage of a quantity, including increases and discounts.
models.draw: One bar as 100%. Cut it into ten parts of 10% each if that helps, then shade the percentage asked for.

example.q: A bag costs $120. It is sold at a 20% discount. How much is paid?
steps: The bar is 100%, which is $120.
A 20% discount means 80% is paid.

models.trap: Working out the discount and stopping. The question asked what is paid, not what was saved. Also watch percentages OF different things: 20% off then 10% off is not 30% off.

models.name: Number and value
models.when: Items have both a count and a price or a value each.
models.draw: Two separate rows: one for how many, one for how much. Keep them apart, or you will multiply the wrong pair.

example.q: Mei has 30 coins, all 20-cent and 50-cent pieces, worth $9.60 altogether. How many are 50-cent coins?
steps: Suppose all 30 coins were 20-cent: 30 × $0.20 = $6.00
The real total is $9.60, so there is $9.60 − $6.00 = $3.60 unaccounted for.
Swapping one 20-cent for one 50-cent adds $0.30 to the total.
Number of swaps: $3.60 ÷ $0.30 = 12

models.trap: Adding the counts to the values. Thirty coins and $9.60 are different kinds of thing and must live on different rows.

models.name: Two cases: excess and shortage
models.when: The same situation is described twice with different numbers, and one version leaves some over while the other falls short.
models.draw: Two models, one for each case, stacked and lined up. The difference between them is caused entirely by the change.

example.q: A teacher shares sweets. Giving each child 3 sweets leaves 4 over. Giving each child 4 sweets leaves her 6 short. How many children are there?
steps: Case 1 uses 3 per child and has 4 spare. Case 2 uses 4 per child and needs 6 more.
Going from case 1 to case 2, each child gets 1 more sweet.
The swing between the two cases is 4 + 6 = 10 sweets.
Each child accounts for 1 of that swing, so there are 10 ÷ 1 = 10 children.
Check: 10 × 3 + 4 = 34 sweets, and 10 × 4 − 6 = 34. The same total both ways.

models.trap: Subtracting the 4 and the 6 instead of adding them. One is a surplus and the other a shortfall, so they are on opposite sides of the true total and the gap between them is their sum.

models.name: Before and after: transfer
models.when: Something moves between two people and the group total stays the same.
words: so that they had equal amounts
models.draw: The before model on top, the after model directly underneath, with the same unit size in both.

example.q: Ken has $84 and Lim has $56. Ken gives Lim some money so that they have the same amount. How much did Ken give?
steps: Nothing enters or leaves, so the total is protected: $84 + $56 = $140
Equal shares: $140 ÷ 2 = $70 each
Ken went from $84 down to $70, so he gave $84 − $70 = $14
Check: Lim goes from $56 to $56 + $14 = $70. Equal.

models.trap: Halving the difference is a shortcut that works here ($28 ÷ 2 = $14) but only when they end exactly equal. Use the total-then-share method and it works every time.

models.name: Working backwards
models.when: The problem ends with a tidy known amount and each earlier step is described as a change.
models.draw: Start at the right-hand end with the known amount and undo one step at a time, writing each intermediate amount above the arrow.

example.q: Raju gave half of what he had left to his sister and finished with $45. Before that he had spent one-third of his money. How much did he start with?
steps: Undo the last step first. He gave away half and kept $45, so before giving he had 2 × $45 = $90.
Undo the step before. $90 is what remained after spending one-third, so $90 is two-thirds of the start.
One-third is $90 ÷ 2 = $45, so the whole is 3 × $45 = $135.
Check forwards: $135 − $45 = $90, then half of $90 is $45. Correct.

models.trap: Undoing the steps in the order they were written. You must undo the LAST thing first, and undoing means the opposite operation.

models.name: Repeated identity
models.when: Two ratios share one person or thing, but that shared quantity has a different number of units in each ratio.
words: A to B is 2 : 3 and B to C is 4 : 5
models.draw: Find the number the shared quantity must become in both: the lowest common multiple. Scale each ratio up to it, then read all three together.

example.q: A : B is 2 : 3 and B : C is 4 : 5. Altogether they have 350. How much does C have?
steps: B is 3 units in the first ratio and 4 in the second. The lowest common multiple of 3 and 4 is 12.
Scale the first ratio by 4: A : B becomes 8 : 12.
Scale the second by 3: B : C becomes 12 : 15.
Now A : B : C is 8 : 12 : 15, which is 35 units in total.
35 units = 350, so 1 unit = 10
C is 15 units: 15 × 10 = 150

models.trap: Writing A : B : C as 2 : 3 : 5 by just joining the ratios up. The 3 and the 4 both mean B, so they have to be made the same first.

models.name: Two unknowns: make one match
models.when: Two different combinations of the same two items are given, each with a total.
models.draw: Write the two situations one above the other. Multiply one or both so that one item appears the same number of times in each, then subtract the rows.

example.q: 3 pens and 2 books cost $31. 5 pens and 2 books cost $43. Find the cost of one book.
steps: Both lines already have exactly 2 books, so no multiplying is needed.
Subtract line 1 from line 2. The books cancel because there are 2 in each.
That leaves 2 pens = $43 − $31 = $12, so 1 pen = $6.
Put it back into line 1: 3 pens = 3 × $6 = $18, so 2 books = $31 − $18 = $13, and 1 book = $6.50.

models.trap: Subtracting when the item you want to cancel does not appear the same number of times in both lines. Make them match first, by multiplying a whole line, before you subtract anything.
